cards.q: A bag has 3 red and 5 blue marbles. One is picked at random. What is the probability that it is red?
cards.why: 3 of the 8 marbles are red: P(red) = 3 ÷ 8 = 3/8. Divide by all the marbles (3 + 5), not just the blue ones.
cards.hook: Probability = the ones you want ÷ all of them.

cards.q: The probability of knocking a coconut off its stand is 0.34. What is the probability of not knocking it off?
cards.why: You either knock it off or you don't, so the two probabilities add to 1: 1 − 0.34 = 0.66.
cards.hook: P(not A) = 1 − P(A).

cards.q: A spinner can land on red, blue or green. P(red) = 0.2 and P(blue) = 0.5. What is P(green)?
cards.why: The three probabilities add to 1: 1 − 0.2 − 0.5 = 0.3.
cards.hook: All the outcomes' probabilities add up to 1.

cards.q: Of 200 babies born in a hospital, 104 were boys. What is the probability that a baby picked at random from them is a boy?
cards.why: P(boy) = boys ÷ all the babies = 104 ÷ 200 = 0.52.
cards.hook: From data: probability = how often it happened ÷ how many in all.

cards.q: The probability that a baby is born on a Tuesday is 0.16. Out of 1300 babies, how many would you expect to be born on a Tuesday?
cards.why: Expected number = total × probability = 1300 × 0.16 = 208.
cards.hook: Expected number = how many times × the probability.

cards.q: Eoin scores a free throw with probability 0.4, and each throw is independent. What is the probability that he scores both of his next two throws?
cards.why: Independent events: multiply. P(score, score) = 0.4 × 0.4 = 0.16.
cards.hook: AND with independent events: multiply.

cards.q: Two fair six-sided dice are thrown. How many different outcomes (like a 2 on the first and a 5 on the second) are there?
cards.why: Each of the 6 scores on the 1st die can go with each of the 6 on the 2nd: 6 × 6 = 36. (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different outcomes.
cards.hook: Two dice: a 6 by 6 table, 36 boxes.

cards.q: Two fair dice are thrown and the scores are added. What is the probability of a total of 7?
cards.why: 7 comes from (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1): 6 of the 36 outcomes, so 6/36. The 11 totals are not equally likely.
cards.hook: Count outcomes in the 36-box table, not the totals.

cards.q: Spinner 1 has 4 equal sections (left/right hand, left/right foot); spinner 2 has 4 equal colours. Both are spun. What is P(right hand and blue)?
cards.why: Right hand and blue is 1 cell of the 4 × 4 table: 1/16. Or multiply, as the spinners are independent: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.
cards.hook: AND: multiply. OR: add (and take off any overlap).

cards.q: Spinner 1 has 4 equal body parts; spinner 2 has 4 equal colours: red, yellow, blue, green. Both are spun (16 outcomes). What is P(red or yellow)?
cards.why: Red is a column of 4 outcomes and yellow is another 4. A spot can't be both, so just add: 4 + 4 = 8 of 16, so 8/16.
cards.hook: OR with no overlap: just add.

cards.q: In a class of 30, 18 play football, 12 play hurling and 5 play both. How many play football or hurling (or both)?
cards.why: Adding 18 + 12 counts the 5 who play both twice, so take them away once: 18 + 12 − 5 = 25.
cards.hook: Football or hurling: add, then take off the "both" once.

cards.q: A Venn diagram shows 40 students: 12 study French only, 9 study French and German, and 8 study German only. How many study neither?
cards.why: The four regions add to 40: 40 − 12 − 9 − 8 = 11 study neither.
cards.hook: All the regions of a Venn diagram add up to the total.

cards.q: On a tree diagram, P(Seán wins match 1) = 0.6 and then P(he loses match 2) = 0.3. What is the probability that he wins match 1 and loses match 2?
cards.why: Multiply along the path Win → Lose: 0.6 × 0.3 = 0.18.
cards.hook: Along a path: multiply. Between paths: add.

cards.q: Mandy picks Balcony or Stalls (equally likely), then Monday, Wednesday or Friday (equally likely). What is the probability she picks Balcony and Wednesday?
cards.why: Multiply along the path Balcony → Wednesday: 1/2 × 1/3 = 1/6. There are 2 × 3 = 6 equally likely paths.
cards.hook: Tree diagram: multiply along the branches.

cards.q: A spinner has 7 sectors of different sizes. The red sector has an angle of 72°. What is the probability of landing on red?
cards.why: Probability is the sector's share of the full turn: 72 ÷ 360 = 1/5.
cards.hook: Spinner probability = angle ÷ 360°.

cards.q: A game pays €10 with probability 0.2 and nothing otherwise. What is the expected prize?
cards.why: Expected value = each prize × its probability, added: 10 × 0.2 + 0 × 0.8 = €2.
cards.hook: Expected value: multiply each value by its probability, then add.

cards.q: Jena pays €1 to play a game. Her expected winnings are €0.90 a game. Is the game fair?
cards.right: No: she loses 10c a game on average
wrong: No: she gains 10c a game on average
Yes: she can sometimes win over €1
cards.why: Fair means the expected value equals the cost. €0.90 is less than €1, so on average she loses 10c a game: not fair.
cards.hook: Fair game: expected winnings = the cost to play.

cards.q: 14 cards: 7 green and 7 red. A red card is picked and not put back. What is the probability that the next card picked is green?
cards.why: The red card isn't put back, so 13 cards are left, and all 7 greens are still there: 7/13.
cards.hook: No replacement: the total goes down by 1 after each pick.

cards.q: Cards: green 1 to 7 and red 1 to 7 (14 cards). One card is picked at random. What is the probability that its number is even?
cards.why: The even numbers are 2, 4 and 6, in both colours: G2, G4, G6, R2, R4, R6. That is 6 of the 14 cards: 6/14.
cards.hook: Count every card that fits, in every colour.

cards.q: 30 animals are in a shelter. The probability that one picked at random is a dog is 11/15. How many dogs are there?
cards.hook: Number expected = total × probability.

cards.q: Rohan scores 70% of his free throws. Which is a good reason why his throws might not be independent?
cards.right: Missing one can make him nervous
wrong: He scores 70% of them on average
Each throw is a score or a miss
He takes more than one throw
cards.why: Independent means one throw doesn't change the chance of the next. Nerves after a miss (or confidence after a score) would change it.
cards.hook: Independent: what happened before makes no difference.
keys: doesn't change the chance of the next

cards.q: What is the quickest correct way to find the probability of at least one six in 3 rolls of a fair die?
cards.why: "At least one six" is every result except no six at all, so work out P(no six) and take it away from 1. 3 × 1/6 counts some results twice.
cards.hook: At least one? Find P(none), then take it from 1.

cards.q: Two fair dice are thrown and the scores are added. What is the probability that the total is a prime number?
cards.why: The prime totals are 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11. In the 36-box table they come up 1 + 2 + 4 + 6 + 2 = 15 times: 15/36.
cards.hook: Prime: exactly two factors. 2 is prime; 1 and 9 are not.

cards.q: A spinner numbered 1 to 5 (all equally likely) is spun twice and the two numbers are added. What is the probability of a total of 4 or 5?
cards.hook: Write both orders: (1,3) and (3,1) are different outcomes.

cards.q: Spinner 1 has 4 equal body parts; spinner 2 has 4 equal colours. Both are spun (16 outcomes). What is the probability of right hand or blue?
cards.why: Right hand is a row of 4 cells, blue a column of 4. They share 1 cell, so count it once: 4 + 4 − 1 = 7, so 7/16.
cards.hook: OR: add, then take away the overlap you counted twice.

cards.q: 30 cars: 18 Fords (7 of them red) and 12 Renaults (4 of them red). A car is picked at random. What is the probability that it is a Ford or is not red?
cards.why: Every Ford (18) plus the Renaults that are not red (12 − 4 = 8): 18 + 8 = 26, so 26/30. Fords that aren't red are already in the 18.
cards.hook: OR: count everything in either group, each car only once.

cards.q: 100 customers: 42 bought vanilla, 37 bought a cone, and 45 bought neither. How many bought vanilla in a cone (both)?
cards.why: 100 − 45 = 55 are in the circles. 42 + 37 = 79 counts "both" twice, so both = 79 − 55 = 24.
cards.hook: The two circles added − the people in the circles = the overlap.

cards.q: 50 people: 12 own a cat only, 18 own a dog only, 10 own both and 10 own neither. What percentage own only one of the two animals?
cards.why: Only one animal = cat only + dog only = 12 + 18 = 30. Then 30 ÷ 50 × 100 = 60%.
cards.hook: "Only" means the part of a circle outside the overlap.

cards.q: P(Seán wins match 1) = 0.6 and P(he wins match 2) = 0.7, independently. What is the probability that he loses both matches?
cards.hook: Losing is "not winning": 1 − p on each branch, then multiply.

cards.q: P(Seán wins match 1) = 0.6 and P(he wins match 2) = 0.7, independently. What is the probability that he wins at least one match?
cards.why: At least one win is everything except losing both: 1 − 0.4 × 0.3 = 1 − 0.12 = 0.88.
cards.hook: At least one = 1 − P(none of them).

cards.q: A game pays €20 with probability 0.1, €5 with probability 0.3, and €0 otherwise. What is the expected prize?
cards.hook: Don't average the prizes: weight each one by its probability.

cards.q: A game costs €1.50 to play. You win €5 with probability 0.2, and nothing otherwise. On average, what happens to a player each game?
cards.why: Expected winnings: 5 × 0.2 = €1. It costs €1.50, so €1 − €1.50 = −50c: a player loses 50c a game on average.
cards.hook: Compare the expected value with the price of a go.

cards.q: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue sweets. Two are taken, one after the other, without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
cards.why: 1st red: 5/8. One red has gone, so 2nd red: 4/7. Multiply: 5/8 × 4/7 = 20/56 (= 5/14).
cards.hook: Without replacement: one fewer on the top and on the bottom.

cards.q: Cards: green 1 to 7 and red 1 to 7. The first card picked is G3 and it is not put back. What is the probability that the second card is a different colour and a different number?
cards.why: 13 cards are left. A different colour means red; a different number rules out R3. That leaves 7 − 1 = 6 red cards: 6/13.
cards.hook: Two conditions: count only the cards that pass both.

cards.q: Each shot hits the target with probability 0.2, independently. What is the probability that the first hit is on the 3rd shot?
cards.why: First hit on the 3rd shot means miss, miss, hit: 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.128. Only one order fits.
cards.hook: "First time on the 3rd": write out the order, then multiply.

cards.q: The probability that a person has blue eyes is 0.7. Four people are picked at random. What is the probability that the 4th is the only one with blue eyes?
cards.why: Not, not, not, blue: 0.3 × 0.3 × 0.3 × 0.7 = 0.0189. The question says which person, so there is just one order.
cards.hook: Told which one? One order. Not told? Count the orders.

cards.q: Rohan scores a free throw with probability 0.6, independently. What is the probability that he scores exactly 2 of his next 3 throws?
cards.why: One miss, and it can be the 1st, 2nd or 3rd throw: 3 orders, each 0.6 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.144. So 3 × 0.144 = 0.432.
cards.hook: Exactly 2 of 3: the odd one out can be in 3 places, so × 3.

cards.q: The probability of rain on any day is 0.3, independently. What is the probability of rain on at least one of the next two days?
cards.why: At least one is everything except no rain on both days: 1 − 0.7 × 0.7 = 1 − 0.49 = 0.51.
cards.hook: At least once? Work out "never", then take it from 1.

cards.q: Daily sales: €100 on a wet day (50% of days), €200 on a dull day (30%), €400 on a sunny day (20%). What are the expected daily sales?
cards.hook: Turn percentages into decimals first: 30% = 0.3.

cards.q: A team takes 6 shots that each score 10% of the time, and 3 shots that each score 40% of the time. What is the expected number of goals?
cards.why: Each shot is worth its probability: 6 × 0.1 + 3 × 0.4 = 0.6 + 1.2 = 1.8 goals.
cards.hook: Expected total = number × probability for each kind, added.
